Out of everything posted about FSD v15 so far, one line from @elonmusk deserves way more attention than it's getting: "This is real-time AI video generation (no gaming engine!) using just half of one AI4 TRIP accelerator. Let that sink in …" 🔥 Half of one accelerator is the part worth sitting with. Once you see the numbers behind it, Reality View stops looking like a fancy new screen and starts looking like one of the most impressive things Tesla has ever shipped. 🎬 THE SCREEN IS NOW GENERATED LIVE For years, FSD's screen worked like a video game. Software took a list of what the car detected and dropped stock 3D models in the right spots: a gray car here, a lane line there. Reality View tosses that playbook out the window. The car's AI now generates the video itself, frame after frame, as you drive, with no game engine anywhere in the loop. Better yet, the picture comes from the same end-to-end model that's doing the driving. That's the single neural network that turns camera video into steering and braking, and now it paints your screen, too. ⚙️ WHAT A TRIP ACTUALLY IS The standard AI4 computer carries two self-driving chips, and each chip packs three custom neural processors Tesla calls TRIP accelerators. That's six in all. And that's where Reality View gets made: right on the self-driving computer, instead of the infotainment chip that runs your maps and music. Each TRIP is basically an arena packed with tiny calculators, all cranking through the multiply-and-add math that neural networks run on. Teardowns count 9,216 of them per TRIP, lined up in a 96-by-96 grid and firing 2.2 billion times a second. Each calculator handles two operations per tick, so one TRIP works out to 9,216 × 2 × 2.2 billion, or roughly 40 trillion operations every second. Half of one comes to about 20 trillion, roughly a twelfth of the whole computer's neural muscle. 📏 WHY THAT NUMBER IS RIDICULOUS Twenty trillion operations per second sounds enormous, until you see what else runs on that kind of budget. The Neural Engine inside Apple's iPhone 15 Pro is rated at 35 trillion operations per second. So on paper, the slice of compute painting Reality View has less raw AI muscle than the AI chip in a 2023 phone. Companies don't all count these numbers the same way, so it's a ballpark, but it shows just how little compute this is. At the other end of the scale sits Nvidia's H100, one of the data-center workhorses powering today's AI boom. It's rated at about 1,979 trillion 8-bit operations per second in its standard mode, the same kind of math a TRIP runs, which puts half a TRIP at roughly 1% of one H100. That gap matters because AI video is one of the toughest jobs in AI. Many AI video generators still take minutes to produce a single clip, as the researchers behind the real-time system MotionStream point out. Even MotionStream, built specifically for speed, streams roughly 17 to 29 frames per second at 480p, and about 10 at 720p, while eating up an entire H100. Meanwhile, Tesla is streaming a live, photorealistic view of the real road on roughly 1% of that chip's rated power, inside a moving car. In other words, Reality View runs on less compute than a phone's AI chip, inside a computer whose main job is driving. There's a fair asterisk here. Those research models dream up whole scenes from a prompt or a single image, while Tesla's renderer starts with a driving brain that already knows exactly what's around the car. Tesla also hasn't shared the view's resolution or frame rate. And even on the most generous estimates of AI4's power, half a TRIP still works out to only about 2% of one H100. Either way, live generated video on a sliver of a car computer would have sounded like science fiction not long ago. 🔍 HOW IT CAN BE THIS CHEAP Tesla hasn't spelled out how it works, but it has left plenty of breadcrumbs. FSD's network has been building its own 3D picture of the world for a while now, something Tesla showed off at the ICCV conference in October 2025. That picture includes 3D Gaussians, millions of soft little blobs of color that can rebuild a scene you can view from any angle. Tesla also built its own Gaussian splatting system that can rebuild a scene from the car's cameras in a fraction of a second. Reality View streams its picture from a virtual camera that can sit anywhere above the car, and showing a scene from an angle no real camera has is exactly what those 3D blobs are great at. Even Elon seems to like that theory: he called a description of Reality View as a neural, Gaussian-splat digital twin "pretty accurate", and it lines up with every other clue. If that's the trick, the hard part is done before the screen ever needs a picture. The driving brain understands the scene, and the visualization just paints what it already knows. That would explain the other shocker. Reality View swapped every separate signal behind the old screen for one end-to-end visualization, and it still uses less compute than the bare-bones 2020 visualization did. 🚗 WHY TESLA CARES SO MUCH v15 is Tesla's large model, built to squeeze every ounce of performance out of HW4. On a chip working that hard, a screen that costs half of one TRIP leaves nearly everything else for the driving. And it's a flex, too. The AI4 computer costs about $650 by Elon's own figure, and that same box now drives the car and paints live video of the world at the same time. This is only the start. Elon says Tesla vehicles will share traffic knowledge and combine it with Grok's real-time 𝕏 feed, even giving you a heads-up about what's happening at your destination. A view this cheap to generate is the perfect canvas for that kind of shared knowledge. Elon asked everyone to let that sink in, and the math earns it: half of one accelerator in a $650 computer is painting the real world live while FSD drives.

SpaceX is planning an absolutely massive 6-gigawatt supercomputing campus in Arizona, designed to operate with ZERO industrial water consumption And the engineering behind this is absolutely insane The proposed campus near Willcox includes: • 747 acres of land • Nine supercomputing buildings, each ~493,000 sq ft • Up to 6 GW of electrical demand across four phases • Up to 24 GWh of battery energy storage • Dry cooling without conventional cooling towers • ZERO industrial groundwater use under its proposed operating plan • Just 7–10 acre-feet of estimated annual operational water consumption • ~$3.6 BILLION in planned grid infrastructure upgrades • ~1,000 permanent jobs and up to 5,500 construction workers All of this is being planned in the middle of the Arizona desert Building superintelligence infrastructure at this scale goes far beyond installing millions of GPUs It means securing enormous amounts of electricity, building advanced cooling systems, expanding the power grid and solving engineering challenges that come with operating at gigawatt scale A single 6 GW campus with 24 GWh of battery storage, designed to operate with minimal on-site water consumption SpaceX is taking superintelligence infrastructure to an entirely different level

FSD V12 Introduced end-to-end neural-network driving. FSD V13 built on that and reduced interventions. FSD V15 will bring: • Pothole avoidance • AI-based mapping and navigation rather than relying on conventional third-party maps. • A new user interface that will re-render reality in a "mind-bending way." • Fleet intelligence that incorporates driving information collected across Tesla vehicles. • Voice integration, allowing drivers to request different routes conversationally (likely through Grok). • Improved parking, destination handling and trip planning. • 10x parameter count increase • New lane change and exiting behavior • And eventually (2027 for Model Y), FSD Unsupervised for personal cars (Tesla's robotaxis already run V15, and the personal Cybercabs being delivered next month likely will too).

Starlink helped save a young man’s life in remote Myanmar. After a landmine blast in Kayah State, his injuries were beyond what the medic on the ground could treat alone. Using Starlink, the team sent photos and videos to a surgeon in Germany, who guided the medic through emergency procedures. Free Burma Rangers says this helped save his life and what remained of his leg. For remote communities with no mobile signal, Starlink can put life-saving expertise within reach, even when the surgeon is thousands of miles away.
